passage: In Durban, Zanele's little brother Pablo had started crying whenever Gogo came to visit, because Gogo always let Zanele help in the kitchen but said Pablo was too small. On Sunday, Zanele saw his face crumple again as Gogo handed her the wooden spoon. For a second she wanted to keep it; stirring the stew was her special job. Then she knelt down. "Pablo, you can shell the peas. That's important too." Gogo raised an eyebrow, then nodded and showed Pablo how to press the pod with his thumb. He dropped half on the floor. At lunch, Gogo told the story of her own big sister, who once let her stir the pot and nearly burnt the house down.

qa.q: What job did Zanele give Pablo in the kitchen?
qa.a: She asked him to shell the peas.

qa.q: What was Zanele feeling when Gogo handed her the wooden spoon?
qa.a: She wanted to keep her special stirring job, but she also felt sorry for Pablo when she saw his face crumple, so she had mixed feelings.

qa.q: How could Gogo help both children feel valued on her visits?
qa.a: She could give each child a real task of their own and teach them different skills, so neither feels left out.

qa.q: What is it like for Pablo to be handed the peas?
qa.a: He probably feels included and proud to have an important job, even if he drops half of them. 🥺

grounding: It shows a child handling sibling rivalry by including a younger brother, while a grandparent teaches and shares her own sibling story.

passage: Damini was nine when her grandfather moved into the old-age home near her school. On Saturdays she went with her little sister Harsha to visit. The common room smelled of Dettol and tea. Harsha was six and kept running off to press the lift buttons. Damini felt her face burn; the nurses were watching. "Harsha, sit," she hissed. Dadu only laughed. "Let her. Come, Damini, help me with this crossword." He showed her how to count the letters and think of rhymes. When Harsha came back, bored, Damini gave her the pencil to fill the easy boxes. Dadu winked at Damini, as if she had done something very grown-up.

qa.q: What did Harsha keep running off to do?
qa.a: She kept running off to press the lift buttons.

qa.q: Why did Damini feel her face burn when Harsha ran around?
qa.a: She was embarrassed because the nurses were watching and she felt responsible for her little sister's behaviour.

qa.q: What worked in the way Damini handled Harsha by the end?
qa.a: Instead of only scolding, she gave Harsha a small task with the pencil, so her sister could join in with Dadu instead of running off.

qa.q: How might Dadu see his granddaughters' visits?
qa.a: He seems to enjoy them, laughing at Harsha's energy and using the crossword to teach Damini, so the visits likely brighten his week.

grounding: It shows a child caring for a younger sibling and learning from a grandparent during visits to a care home.

passage: I'm Francis, from next door. Sumit, who's eleven, has two little twin brothers, and I used to hear him shouting at them through the wall. Last summer his grandmother came from Kerala for three months. Every evening I'd see her on their porch teaching Sumit how to peel mangoes in one long strip. The twins would try to grab the knife, and she'd hand them the seeds to suck instead. Sumit started doing the same thing when she wasn't there. Once I saw him split his biscuit into three. I don't know what he felt, but the shouting got less. When his grandmother left, he stood at the gate for a long time after the taxi turned.

qa.q: What did Sumit's grandmother teach him on the porch?
qa.a: She taught him how to peel mangoes in one long strip.

qa.q: What does Sumit standing at the gate after the taxi left suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt sad to see his grandmother go and had grown close to her during her stay.

qa.q: What could Sumit's parents do to keep the change going after the grandmother left?
qa.a: They could notice and praise his patience with the twins, and help him keep in touch with his grandmother by phone.

qa.q: Why might the twins see Sumit differently after the summer?
qa.a: Since he now shares biscuits and shouts less, they may start seeing him as someone kind to turn to, not just a bossy big brother.

grounding: A neighbour observes a boy learning patience with younger siblings from his visiting grandmother.

passage: Friday: Madhav, ten, came home to find his clay volcano squashed. Shankar, six, stood beside it with guilty fingers. 'You RUIN everything!' Madhav yelled, and Shankar wailed. Thatha watched from his chair and said nothing. Sunday: Thatha called Madhav to the terrace with a paper kite. 'When your father was small, he broke my radio,' he said, tying the string. 'I shouted at him. He didn't touch anything of mine for a year. I missed him.' Madhav was quiet. Wednesday: Shankar crept up to the terrace to watch. Madhav held out the string. 'Hold here. Don't pull too hard.' The kite dipped and rose. Shankar squealed. Thatha smiled from the doorway.

qa.q: What did Madhav's father break when he was small?
qa.a: He broke Thatha's radio.

qa.q: Why do you think Madhav went quiet after Thatha's story?
qa.a: He was probably realising that shouting at Shankar might push his little brother away, as it had in Thatha's story.

qa.q: What did Thatha do that helped without lecturing?
qa.a: He shared a memory about his own mistake and let Madhav reach his own conclusion.

qa.q: How might Shankar see Madhav after the kite day?
qa.a: He might start trusting his big brother again and want to learn more from him. 😊

grounding: Shows sibling rivalry easing as a child learns from his grandfather and cares for his younger brother.

passage: Manjula, my darling, you're angry with your sister over a hair clip? Let me tell you a secret. When I was ten, I had a red ribbon, a gift from my uncle in Bombay, and my little sister Kamu took it for a wedding without asking. I pulled her hair so hard she cried. My Paati sat me down, not angry, and said, 'Devika, you are the elder. Your sister copies you because she wants to be you.' I didn't understand then. Afterwards, I lent Kamu the ribbon for her school day, and she walked like a queen. We braided each other's hair for fifty years. Now, go and see what your sister wants, and why.

qa.q: Where did the red ribbon come from?
qa.a: It was a gift from young Devika's uncle in Bombay.

qa.q: What did Devika's Paati think Kamu was feeling when she took the ribbon?
qa.a: She thought Kamu admired Devika as the elder one and wanted to be like Devika.

qa.q: What does Devika suggest Manjula do about the hair clip?
qa.a: To go to the sister and find out what she wants and why, instead of just staying angry.

qa.q: How might Kamu have felt walking to school with the ribbon?
qa.a: She would likely feel proud and loved, like a queen, because Devika chose to share. 🤍

grounding: An elder recalls sibling rivalry and a lesson from Paati about caring for a younger sibling.

passage:
The rain came down so hard that Joseph's parents called: the road was flooded, they'd be two hours late.
Joseph, eleven, was in charge of his cousin Santosh, six, who started crying as soon as the lights flickered.
“Stop crying,” Joseph snapped. “You always cry.” Santosh cried louder.
Joseph took a breath. He remembered how Ammachi calmed them when they were small. He lit a candle, sat next to Santosh, and started telling the story she used to tell about the fisherman and the golden fish.
Santosh stopped crying and leaned against him.
When the parents arrived, both boys were asleep on the sofa.

qa.q: How late did Joseph's parents say they'd be?
qa.a: Two hours late.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel when Santosh started crying?
qa.a: He felt irritated and stressed, snapping at him.

qa.q: What did Joseph do that calmed Santosh?
qa.a: He lit a candle, sat beside him and told Ammachi's story, as she used to.

qa.q: How might Santosh feel leaning against Joseph?
qa.a: He probably feels safe and comforted by his older cousin.

grounding: During a flood delay an eleven-year-old cares for a younger cousin using a grandmother's story.

passage:
Pranav and his sister Disha had fought over the window seat of the car all week, all the way to Nani's flat in Chennai.
That evening, Nani brought out a wooden board with fourteen pits and a bag of cowrie shells. “Pallanguzhi. I played it with my brother when I was your age.”
She taught them both. Pranav, ten, kept losing to Disha. He threw a shell.
Nani said quietly, “My brother used to throw shells too. Then he learned to count ahead.”
Pranav picked up the shell and watched Nani's hands. The next game, he won.
On the way home, he let Disha have the window seat.

qa.q: What did Nani bring out?
qa.a: A wooden board with fourteen pits and a bag of cowrie shells.

qa.q: How did Pranav feel when he kept losing to Disha?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and angry, throwing a shell.

qa.q: What did Nani do that helped Pranav?
qa.a: She calmly shared a story about her brother and taught him to count ahead.

qa.q: How might Disha feel when Pranav gives her the window seat?
qa.a: She probably feels surprised and happy, sensing the rivalry has eased.

grounding: A ten-year-old learns from his grandmother and eases his rivalry with his sister.

passage:
“Ammi, why does she get to sleep with you? I'm your son too.”
Sarika looked up from the baby. “Irfan, come here.”
Irfan, nine, came slowly and sat on the bed.
“When you were a baby, you slept with me too. Every night. You cried if I put you down.”
“Really?”
“Really. She's small now. She needs me close. You need me too, just differently.”
Irfan looked at his sister's tiny fist. “Can I hold her?”
Sarika showed him how to support her head. Irfan held her very still.
“She likes you,” Sarika whispered.
“She's squeezing my finger,” Irfan said, amazed.

qa.q: What did Sarika show Irfan how to do?
qa.a: She showed him how to support the baby's head.

qa.q: How did Irfan feel when he asked why the baby sleeps with Ammi?
qa.a: He felt jealous and left out.

qa.q: What did Sarika say that helped Irfan?
qa.a: She told him he had been cared for the same way and that he still needs her, just differently.

qa.q: How might the baby's arrival feel different for Irfan after holding her?
qa.a: He may feel more connected and protective, and less jealous.

grounding: A nine-year-old moves from jealousy of his baby sister to caring for her with his mother's help.

passage:
When I was ten, I hated my little sister Avni. Everyone said she was cute. Nobody said I was cute.
One day she broke my kite, and I pushed her. She cried. Dadi saw.
Dadi didn't shout. She took me to the terrace and said, "When your father was your age, he pushed his brother too. Then his brother fell sick, and your father sat by his bed every night."
I didn't understand then. But the next week, Avni had fever. I sat by her and read her comics.
My name is Bhupen. Avni and I still fight. But I remember Dadi's story.

qa.q: What did Avni break?
qa.a: Bhupen's kite.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling about Avni being called cute?
qa.a: Bhupen felt jealous and left out.

qa.q: What did Dadi do that helped more than shouting?
qa.a: She shared a family story, which helped Bhupen see what brothers and sisters can mean to each other.

qa.q: How might Avni have felt when Bhupen read her comics?
qa.a: Avni probably felt cared for and surprised that Bhupen was being so kind.

grounding: A young person recalls sibling rivalry and a grandmother's story that changed his actions.

passage:
Class teacher's note.
Preeti is in Class 5. Her mother works night shifts, so Preeti brings her little sister Pema to the pre-primary gate each morning. I've noticed Preeti re-ties Pema's shoelaces, checks her tiffin, and gives her a hug before leaving.
Today Preeti was late for class. When I asked why, she said Pema was crying and wouldn't let go.
Preeti looked worried she'd be in trouble. I told her it was kind of her. I also spoke to the pre-primary teacher, who will meet Pema at the gate from tomorrow so Preeti can get to class on time.
Preeti smiled for the first time today. — Mr Iyer

qa.q: Why does Preeti bring Pema to the gate?
qa.a: Because her mother works night shifts.

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling when she was late for class?
qa.a: Preeti felt worried she'd be in trouble, and probably stressed by Pema's crying.

qa.q: What did Mr Iyer do that helped Preeti?
qa.a: He praised her kindness and arranged for the pre-primary teacher to meet Pema, so Preeti wouldn't carry it alone.

qa.q: How might Pema feel when a teacher meets her at the gate?
qa.a: Pema may feel safer and less scared when Preeti leaves 😊.

grounding: A teacher notes a child caring for her younger sister and arranges support.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Nani came to stay this week. Today she taught me to make rotis. Mine looked like maps of India.
My little brother Ujjwal kept laughing. "That one's Gujarat!"
I was going to throw one at him. But Nani said, "Ujjwal, come, you roll one too." His was even worse. He looked like he'd cry.
Nani said, "My first rotis were like stones. My mother fed them to the cow." We all laughed.
Then she showed us both how to turn the roti on the tawa. We made twelve together.
I want to learn all her recipes before she goes back.
— Simran

qa.q: How many rotis did they make together?
qa.a: Twelve.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling when his roti was even worse?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt embarrassed and close to tears after laughing at Simran's roti.

qa.q: What did Nani do that turned the rivalry around?
qa.a: She included Ujjwal, shared a funny story about her own mistakes, and taught both of them together.

qa.q: How might Nani feel teaching Simran and Ujjwal?
qa.a: Nani probably feels happy and close to them, passing on her skills and making them laugh.

grounding: In her diary a child writes about learning from her grandmother and a moment with her brother.

passage:
In the Kinnaur village, Dolma's mother went to the apple orchard at dawn, so Dolma had to get her little sister Vinita ready for school. Vinita wouldn't put on her socks. Dolma was going to be late again.
"You always get the window seat on the bus. You always get Mola's stories first," Dolma snapped.
Their grandmother, Mola, was sitting by the stove. She said nothing, just handed Dolma a warm roti and pointed at Vinita's feet. "Cold socks. Warm them first."
Dolma held the socks near the stove. Vinita put them on at once.
That evening, Mola told the story to Dolma first. "Big sisters learn things first," she said. "Then they teach." Dolma sat a bit taller.

qa.q: Where did Dolma's mother go at dawn?
qa.a: She went to the apple orchard.

qa.q: Why did Dolma snap at Vinita?
qa.a: Dolma felt stressed about being late and jealous that Vinita always seemed to get the window seat and Mola's stories first.

qa.q: What small step helped with the socks, and what does it teach about caring for younger ones?
qa.a: Warming the socks first worked, because looking for the reason behind a little one's fuss often works better than pushing.

qa.q: How might Mola see the tension between her two granddaughters?
qa.a: Mola seems to understand both girls and, rather than scolding, quietly gives Dolma a way to feel valued as the elder.

grounding: Illustrates a child managing sibling jealousy, caring for a younger sister and learning from a grandparent.

passage:
For weeks before Lucia day in Uppsala, Vera had wanted to be Lucia at school. The teacher chose her little sister's class instead, and Ingrid got the crown of candles.
Vera slammed her bedroom door. "She's seven! She'll drop it."
Mormor came in with flour on her hands. "Come and help with the saffron buns. I need someone who can shape an S properly."
They twisted dough together. Mormor told her she had never been Lucia either. "I was the one who held the matches. Still remember it."
On the morning, Ingrid's crown slipped as she walked. Vera, in the front row, saw Ingrid's panicked face, stepped out and fixed a pin, fast. Ingrid walked on, glowing.
Afterwards Ingrid gave Vera the best bun.

qa.q: What did Mormor ask Vera to help make?
qa.a: Mormor asked her to help with the saffron buns.

qa.q: Why did Vera slam her bedroom door?
qa.a: Vera felt jealous and disappointed that Ingrid got the crown she had wanted for weeks.

qa.q: How did Mormor help Vera without scolding her?
qa.a: She gave Vera a job that needed her skill and shared that she had never been Lucia either, which eased the sting.

qa.q: What was it like for Ingrid when Vera fixed her crown?
qa.a: Ingrid was probably scared the crown would fall and then relieved and grateful that her big sister helped.

grounding: Shows a child moving from sibling rivalry to caring for a younger sister, helped by a grandparent's story.

passage:
Grandparents' Day at school fell in the last week of December, with a heater in the hall and tea in paper cups. Salma had practised a speech about her Dadi. Her little brother, from Class 2, kept grabbing the microphone and saying "My Dadi!" before her.
"He's ruining it," Salma hissed to her friend Gargi.
Dadi pulled Salma close. "When your Abbu was small, he did the same to his sister. She let him say one line, and then she said the rest. Everyone remembers her speech."
So Salma knelt, let her brother say "My Dadi makes the best sheer khurma," and then stood up and gave hers. The hall laughed at his line and clapped at hers. Gargi gave her a thumbs up.

qa.q: What line did Salma's little brother say into the microphone?
qa.a: He said, "My Dadi makes the best sheer khurma."

qa.q: What was Salma feeling when she hissed to Gargi?
qa.a: Salma felt frustrated and annoyed that her brother kept grabbing the microphone and, she thought, ruining her speech.

qa.q: Which idea from Dadi worked, and why?
qa.a: Letting her brother say one line first worked, because he got his turn and stopped competing, and Salma still gave her speech.

qa.q: How might Dadi feel watching both grandchildren speak about her?
qa.a: Dadi probably feels proud and loved, and pleased that her story helped Salma choose patience over a fight.

grounding: Illustrates a child handling sibling rivalry by learning from a grandparent's advice at a school event.

passage:
I'm Tanuja from the flat opposite, and I watched Jomon all through Christmas week.
Jomon, eleven, and his little brother Abel fought constantly over the one bicycle. Once Abel pushed him, and Jomon yelled, "You ruin everything!"
But on Christmas Eve I saw Jomon on the balcony with his grandfather, Appachan, making a paper star lantern. Appachan showed him how to fold the points. Jomon kept glancing at Abel, who was sulking inside.
Then Jomon called him. "Abel, hold the frame. You're good at holding still."
Abel came running. The star went up crooked, and all three laughed. I don't know what made Jomon change his mind, but the bicycle fight didn't happen that evening.

qa.q: What were Jomon and Appachan making on the balcony?
qa.a: They were making a paper star lantern.

qa.q: What might Jomon have been feeling when he kept glancing at Abel?
qa.a: He may have felt guilty or sorry for yelling, and wanted to include his little brother.

qa.q: How could Appachan help the brothers get along?
qa.a: He could keep giving them projects that need both of them, like the lantern, where each has a job.

qa.q: What is it like for Abel to be invited to hold the frame?
qa.a: Abel probably feels happy and included after sulking, and proud to be told he is good at something.

grounding: Shows a child moving from sibling rivalry to caring for his younger brother while learning from a grandparent.
